sentences: You are at the Lahori Gate, the way in.
Shah Jahan built it facing Lahore, which is how it got its name.
The wall you are looking at ends in bastions at both corners, each one crowned by a pavilion.
The screen wall in front of the gate is not his.
Aurangzeb added it, and his father wrote to him from prison in Agra to say that he had made the Fort a bride and set a veil before her face.
It is not clear whether that was meant as a compliment.
Every fifteenth of August the Prime Minister speaks to the country from the rampart above you.
The Lahori Gate, the main way in, set in the west wall and named for the road to Lahore.
The wall ends in a projecting bastion at each corner and each bastion is crowned by a pavilion.
That is a defensive shape being used decoratively, which is most of what Shah Jahan does here.
The screen wall in front of you is a barbican, added later by Aurangzeb, and it works by forcing an attacker to turn a corner under fire.
It also blocks the view straight down the axis, which is why Shah Jahan complained that his son had put a veil on the building.
The slope below the wall, the glacis, is British and was added after 1857.
This is the front door.
It points towards Lahore, which is why it is called the Lahori Gate.
The emperor's son built the extra wall in front of it, and his father wrote him a letter saying he had put a veil on the building.
Every year on the fifteenth of August, somebody stands up there and talks to the whole country.
This is the Chatta Chowk, the covered bazaar.
It runs two hundred and thirty feet, and there are thirty two arched rooms along the sides of it.
They were shops then and they are shops now.
Halfway along, the roof opens into an octagonal court about thirty feet across, and that is the only thing letting light and air into the whole passage.
Look up at the plaster around that opening and you can still find traces of the painting that once covered it.
Fergusson called this the noblest entrance belonging to any palace still standing.
The Chatta Chowk, the covered bazaar you walk through to reach the palace.
The vault overhead is doing the structural work, which is why the walls could be opened into thirty two shop fronts without weakening anything.
Halfway along, the builders stopped the vault and opened an octagonal court.
That opening is the entire lighting and ventilation system for the passage.
Look at the plaster inside it for what is left of the original painted decoration.
You are in a shopping street with a roof on it.
There are thirty two little rooms along the sides, and they were shops four hundred years ago.
They are still shops.
The hole in the roof in the middle is there to let the light in.
The Naubat Khana, the drum house.
This was the main way into the court of the Diwan-i-Aam, and it was the point at which you got off your elephant.
Everybody did, except princes of the blood royal.
It was called the Hathia Pol, the elephant gate, for that reason.
Above the gateway there is an open hall of five arched bays, and that is where the musicians sat.
They played at fixed hours, so this building told the time as well as guarding the door.
The Naubat Khana, the drum house, and the main entrance to the court of the Diwan-i-Aam.
It is three storeys, and the top one is an open hall of five arched bays.
It is open because it had to carry sound.
Musicians played from up there at fixed hours.
The gateway below it is twenty nine feet high, which is the height of a man on an elephant, and that is what it was cut for.
The building is a gate, a guardhouse and a musical instrument at the same time.
This is the drum house.
Musicians sat in the room at the top and played at certain times of day, so people knew what time it was.
It was also where you had to get off your elephant.
Only princes were allowed to ride through.
You are standing in front of the Diwan-i-Aam, the hall of public audience.
Shah Jahan finished it in 1648 and held his first court here soon after.
It is built entirely of red sandstone, and it was once covered in gilding and painted plaster, all of which is gone.
Inside, four columns carry each arch, in seven bays across three aisles.
In the middle of the far wall there is a recess raised above the floor.
That is where the Emperor sat.
The lawn in front of you stands in for a courtyard that ran five hundred and sixty feet.
The shrubberies mark where the arcades used to be, and every morning they were full of men waiting to be seen.
The Diwan-i-Aam, the hall of public audience, where the Emperor showed himself to whoever had come.
Inside it is three aisles of seven bays, and each bay is four columns carrying an engrailed arch, the scalloped profile you can see along the front.
A deep chhajja, the projecting stone eave, runs along three faces and throws the wall into shadow.
The hall was never meant to stand alone.
A court ran in front of it, arcaded on all sides, where the nobles waited.
None of the stone was meant to be seen either.
It was gilded and covered in painted stucco, and all of that is gone.
This is where the emperor listened to people.
Anyone could come and ask him for something.
You stood in the courtyard and waited your turn.
He sat in that stone box in the middle of the back wall, up above everybody.
The whole hall used to be gold and painted, not plain red like it is now.
This is the Rang Mahal, the painted palace.
It is named for the colour that once covered the inside of these walls, and almost none of it is left.
Shah Jahan knew it as the Imtiyaz Mahal, the palace of distinction, and it was the largest apartment in the imperial household.
A marble channel runs the length of the floor, and at its centre sits a basin cut from a single block of Makrana marble.
The ceiling was silver first, then copper, then wood.
Each replacement was a smaller claim than the one before.
Behind you, between this hall and the back of the Diwan-i-Aam, there was a walled garden with a tank at its centre.
It lay buried until 1911, when it was uncovered again.
The Rang Mahal, the palace of colour, where the women of the imperial household lived.
A long hall rather than a square one, with a smaller room closed off at each end.
A marble channel runs the full length of the floor, and at its centre is a basin cut from a single block of Makrana marble.
Cutting a basin that size from one block is a quarrying problem before it is a carving problem.
There is a range of rooms underground on the west side, which is how you cool a building in Delhi without machinery.
Rang Mahal means the coloured palace, because the inside was painted all over.
Almost none of the colour is left, so you have to imagine it.
There is a stream of water running along the floor, and in the middle of it a bowl carved out of one enormous piece of marble.
The ceiling was silver once.
Then copper.
Then wood.
This is the Khas Mahal, where the Emperor actually lived.
Three rooms face the Diwan-i-Khas, three more behind them were the sleeping chamber, and the hall alongside held the wardrobe and the treasury.
The walls carry a dado of inlaid marble.
Look at the screen on the north wall.
It was cut out of a single slab, and the pattern in it is a pair of scales hanging over a crescent moon among stars and clouds.
That is the Mizan-i-Adl, the scales of justice, and it was put where anyone bringing a complaint would see it.
The inscriptions on the arches were written by Sadullah Khan, who ran the government of Shah Jahan until he died in 1656.
The Khas Mahal, the Emperor's own apartment: a prayer room, a sleeping chamber and a sitting hall in a row.
The walls carry an inlaid marble dado, which is stone set into stone rather than paint on plaster.
The north and south walls of the central room are closed by marble screens cut from single slabs.
A screen like that has to be carved in place, in the plane of the wall, because it cannot be assembled from pieces.
The one on the north carries a pair of scales over a crescent moon, among stars and clouds.
This is where the emperor slept.
Look at the stone screen in the wall.
Somebody cut all those holes out of one flat piece of marble by hand.
There is a picture in it of a weighing scale hanging under a moon.
That was a promise that he would be fair to people.
This is the Diwan-i-Khas, the hall of private audience.
Shah Jahan finished it in 1648, and a nineteenth century surveyor called it the most highly ornamented building he ever put up.
Look at the lower part of the piers.
Every piece of coloured stone in them was cut to fit a socket chiselled out of the marble.
Higher up, the arches were gilded and painted.
The marble channel running down the centre of the floor was called the Nahr-i-Bihisht, the stream of paradise.
The peacock throne stood on the dais in this room until 1739, when Nadir Shah carried it away to Persia.
He accepted the surrender of the Mughal Emperor here first, and took the throne afterwards.
The Diwan-i-Khas, the hall of private audience, where the Emperor met the people he chose to meet.
The ceiling is flat and it is carried on engrailed arches, so the arches are decorative and the load is going down the piers.
The lower part of each pier is pietra dura, coloured stone cut to fit sockets chiselled out of the marble.
The upper parts were gilded and painted instead, because inlay that high up would never be read.
A marble water channel runs through the centre of the hall and cools it as it goes.
This room was only for important visitors.
There used to be a golden throne here shaped like a peacock, covered in jewels.
In 1739 a king from Persia took Delhi, took the throne, and carried it away.
It never came back.
The coloured flowers on the pillars are not painted.
Every petal is a piece of stone cut to fit a hole.
The Hammam, the royal baths.
Three main rooms divided by corridors, and every surface you would have touched is marble inlaid with coloured stone.
The pavements, the reservoirs, the slabs the steam came through, and the walls up to waist height.
The room facing the river was where you undressed.
It has three fountain basins in it, and one of them ran rose water.
Some of the coloured glass in the window lattice is original.
Heating this building was said to take a hundred and twenty five maunds of firewood, which is something over four tonnes.
The Hammam, the royal baths, three apartments off a corridor.
Everything you would have touched is marble inlaid with coloured stone: the pavements, the reservoirs, the vapour slabs and the walls to waist height.
The vapour slabs are the point.
Heat came up through the floor and the stone held it.
The room facing the river is where clothes came off, and it has three fountain basins, one of them for a rose water spray.
The window keeps its marble lattice and some of its original coloured glass.
These were the royal baths.
Hot steam came up through the floor, and the stone stayed warm.
One of the fountains squirted rose water instead of ordinary water.
Keeping it all hot took about four tonnes of firewood.
The Moti Masjid, the pearl mosque.
Aurangzeb built it about eleven years after the Fort was finished, and it cost a hundred and sixty thousand rupees of the time.
It was private.
The Emperor prayed here, and so did the women of the household, who reached it by their own passage through the north wall.
The doors on the east side are plated with copper.
The domes are wrong.
The originals were covered in gilded copper, they were damaged in 1857, and what you are looking at is the repair.
The Moti Masjid, the pearl mosque, the Emperor's own place of prayer.
Aurangzeb added it in 1659, eleven years after the Fort was finished.
It sits inside its own walled enclosure, which is how you fit a mosque into a palace without breaking either.
The main door is in the east wall and is plated with copper, and a second passage through the north wall let the women of the household reach it separately.
The domes are not the originals.
Those were sheathed in gilded copper and were lost in 1857.
This is a tiny private mosque, just for the emperor and his family.
It is called the Pearl Mosque.
The domes on top used to be covered in shiny gold coloured metal.
They were broken in a war and these ones are the replacements.
The Hayat Bakhsh Bagh.
The name means life bestowing.
It was laid out with the rest of the Fort, quartered by water channels in the Persian manner.
Then it was lost.
By 1902 the whole garden was under earth, rubble and roads, and the channels had almost completely gone.
Digging it back out took from 1904 to 1911.
Only half of it came back, because the army had built barracks on the other half.
Almost everything you can see of the causeways and the channels is reconstruction.
The Hayat Bakhsh Bagh, the life bestowing garden, laid out as a charbagh.
That means it is quartered by water channels crossing at the centre, so the plan is a cross.
The water is structural, not decorative.
It sets the axes, feeds the planting and cools the air.
By 1902 all of it was buried under earth, rubble and roads, and the channels had effectively vanished.
Reconstruction ran from 1904 to 1911 and recovered half the garden.
The other half was under barracks, which is why it stops where it does.
This is a garden, and its name means life giving.
It was built as four squares with water running between them in stone channels.
Then everyone forgot about it and it got buried under mud and roads.
People dug it back up about a hundred years ago, but they only found half of it.
Mumtaz Mahal, eighty eight feet by eighty two.
This was one of the apartments of the seraglio, the part of the palace where the women of the household lived.
The lower parts of the walls and piers are marble, and traces of the painted and glass decoration that covered the rest have been uncovered.
The gilded chhatris that stood at the corners of the roof are gone.
What happened to this building afterwards is roughly what happened to the whole Fort.
It was a prison after 1857, then a sergeants mess, and it is a museum now.
The Mumtaz Mahal, one of the palaces of the harem, and today the Fort's museum.
Very nearly square, and the lower parts of the walls and piers are marble.
The rest was painted and glazed decoration, traces of which have been uncovered.
The gilded chhatris that stood at the four corners of the roof are gone, and much of what you see is a repair from 1911.
It has been a palace apartment, a prison, a sergeants mess and a museum, and the fabric shows all four.
The women of the emperor's family lived in this building.
The bottom of the walls is marble and the rest was painted.
There were little gold domes on the corners of the roof once.
Afterwards it was a prison, then a room for soldiers, and now it is a museum.
The tomb of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya.
The survey calls it one of the most sacred shrines in India, and it has been added to by almost everyone who ever held Delhi.
Firoz Shah Tughlaq repaired the first building and put up a hall for the congregation that had not existed before.
Nothing of his work survives.

What you are looking at was built in 1562 by Faridun Khan, given its verandah ninety years later by the governor of Shahjahanabad, and given the marble rail round the grave by a nobleman of Hyderabad in 1882.
Three hundred years of people adding to one room.
The tomb of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya, and it is small: thirty one feet nine inches square on the outside.
Almost all of that is the verandah, which is marble paved, six feet nine inches deep, and open through five arches on every side.
The chamber inside is only fifteen feet eight.
Look up at the dome.
It is the bulbous kind, it stands on an eight sided drum, and it is striped vertically in black marble, which is unusual enough that you will not mistake this roof for another.
The arches are usually hung with heavy cotton curtains, so the building you see changes with the day.
This is the tomb of Nizamuddin Auliya, and there is music in front of it almost every week.
A teacher called Nizamuddin was buried here seven hundred years ago, and people have been coming ever since.
Kings kept adding bits to it.
One added the porch you are standing in, another added the silver rail around the grave.
Count the black stripes going up the dome.
If singers are sitting outside, stay and listen for a minute, because that is the oldest thing here.
The tomb of Atgah Khan, finished in 1567.
His real name was Shamsuddin Muhammad, and Atgah Khan is not a name at all: it was the title given to the husband of a royal wet nurse.
He earned that place by pulling Humayun off the field after Sher Shah Sur beat him, and the emperor made his wife nurse to the young Akbar in return.
He rose to be chancellor of the empire, and it killed him.
In 1562 Adham Khan, the son of another of Akbar's nurses, stabbed him in the palace at Agra.
His body was carried to Delhi to lie near the saint, and his son built this over him.
The tomb of Atgah Khan: a single domed chamber, twenty feet square, standing inside its own walled enclosure.
The material is the point: red stone inlaid with marble and with coloured tiles, which is a lot of decoration for a building this small.
There is a deeply recessed arch on each of the four sides.
Three of them are closed with latticed stone screens and only the southern one is a door.
Quranic inscriptions run round all four arches and end with the name of the man who wrote them, Baqi Muhammad.
The doorway inscription names the foreman as well, Ustad Khuda Quli.
This is the tomb of Atgah Khan.
Small building, big story.
The man inside once saved an emperor's life by getting him off a battlefield he had just lost.
As a reward his wife became the baby prince's nurse, and that made his whole family important.
It also made people jealous, and one of them killed him.
Look at the walls: red stone with white marble and coloured tiles pushed into it, like a pattern set into a floor but standing up.
Three of the four archways are filled with stone screens, so there is only one way in.
Chaunsath Khamba, which means sixty four pillars, and they are all in front of you.
This is the tomb of Mirza Aziz Kokaltash, and he built it himself while he was still alive.
Kokaltash means foster brother.
His mother nursed the emperor Akbar, so Mirza Aziz grew up beside him and was treated as family for the rest of his life.
He died in Ahmadabad in 1624 and was carried back here to be buried near his father and near the saint.
Eight more graves inside are said to be his family, and not one of them is inscribed.
Chaunsath Khamba: a hall of marble, sixty seven feet square, divided into twenty five bays and every bay domed.
The pillars are set in pairs, depth-wise, so each side reads as five openings rather than a wall.
Between them the builders hung latticed marble screens about ten feet high, with a door cut in the middle bay of each side.
Above the screens the arches are left open, which is why the light inside moves all day.
This is a tomb built as a pavilion.
Nothing about it is trying to keep you out.
This is Chaunsath Khamba, and the name is a number.
Chaunsath khamba means sixty four pillars, and if you have time you can check.
The man buried here was the emperor's foster brother, which means the same woman fed them both as babies.
At the Mughal court that made you family for life.
He built this whole marble hall for himself before he died, and the walls are stone screens cut full of holes so the wind goes straight through.
The Qutub Minar, two hundred and thirty four feet of it.
It was not built by one person or in one lifetime.
Qutbuddin Aibak built the bottom storey, Iltutmish finished the tower, and in 1368 Firoz Shah rebuilt the top after lightning struck it.
The inscription up there says so in his own words.
A cupola stood on the summit until an earthquake threw it down in 1803.
Its replacement was so disliked that Lord Hardinge had it taken off in 1848, and it is still sitting on the ground nearby.
The Qutub Minar.
The shaft is forty seven feet three inches across at the bottom and nine feet at the top, so it narrows by a factor of five as it climbs.
Five balconies break it into five storeys.
Look at the flutes.

The lowest storey is a twenty four sided polygon of alternating angular and rounded flutes; the second is rounded only; the third goes back to angular; the fourth is plain and uses marble; the fifth alternates marble and red sandstone.
Each storey is a different idea, stacked.
The bands you can see between the balconies are inscriptions wound together with foliage.
This is the Qutub Minar, the tallest brick tower of its kind anywhere, and it took more than a hundred years to finish.
Count the balconies going up.
There are five, and each section between them is carved a different way.
It was built so someone could stand at the top and call people to prayer.
Lightning hit it once and a king had to rebuild the top.
Later an earthquake knocked the little roof off the summit, and that roof is still lying on the ground somewhere near you.
The Quwwatul Islam mosque, built in 1191 by Qutbuddin Aibak.
The inscription over the east gate says the materials of twenty seven temples went into it, and it says so as a boast.
Cunningham worked out what that meant on the ground: the older temple was pulled down to the plinth, and its columns were stood up again to make these colonnades.
So you are inside two buildings at once.
Altamsh doubled it in 1230 and Alauddin Khalji doubled it again ninety years later.
The outer edge of his extension was only found in the excavations of 1911.
The Quwwatul Islam mosque.
The court is a hundred and forty two feet by a hundred and eight, ringed by colonnades of grey stone, four pillars deep on the east and three on the north and south.
The prayer chamber on the west is a hundred and forty seven by forty, with five rows of pillars in it.
The thing to look at is the screen across its front.
Five ogee arches in red and yellow sandstone, carved with Hindu patterns, with bands of naskh lettering running through them.
The carvers were local and the script was not.
You can see both hands on the same stone.
This is the Quwwatul Islam mosque, and it is built out of other buildings.
The writing over the gate says stone from twenty seven temples was used here.
Look closely at the pillars.
Some of them still have the old carvings on them, flowers and bells and little figures, because nobody cut them off.
The mosque got bigger twice after it was built.
The last edge of it stayed lost underground until 1911, when somebody dug it up.
The Alai Minar, and it is a stump because it was never finished.
Alauddin Khalji wanted a tower twice the Qutub Minar in height and twice around.
He got this far and died, and the work stopped the same year.
The survey passes on a story that the marble meant to face it went into Humayun's tomb instead.
If that is true, then a building four miles from here is partly made of this one.
Nobody finished it and nobody took it down either.
The Alai Minar is the only building here you can see the inside of without going in.
What stands is the rubble core.
Every finished tower on this site has one, and every finished tower hides it under dressed stone.
The survey says the architect plainly meant to face this with something better, and the surface you are looking at was never meant to be a surface.
It was going to be twice the Qutub Minar in both height and circumference.
Work out from the base how wide that would have made it.
This is the Alai Minar, the tower nobody ever finished.
A king decided to build one twice as tall and twice as wide as the Qutub Minar next door.
Then he died, and everyone stopped.
What is left is the rough insides, because the smooth stone was never put on the outside.
People say the marble for it was carted off and used on Humayun's tomb instead.
The tomb of Isa Khan, built in 1547, which makes it twenty years older than the emperor's tomb behind you.
Isa Khan Niyazi served Sher Shah Sur, the man who drove Humayun out of India.
When Sher Shah died it was largely Isa Khan who kept his son on the throne of Delhi.
So the Mughals built their mausoleum next door to a man who had fought them.
He built this while he was alive, which was the ordinary thing to do.
Six graves are inside and only his is identified with any confidence.
The tomb of Isa Khan is an octagon, and everything about it says so twice.
A verandah runs the whole way round under a deep chajja carried on heavy stone brackets.
The eight corners are propped with sloping buttresses, which is what gives it that squat, planted look.
Eight chattris on red sandstone columns stand at roof level, one for each side.
The dome is low and wide and springs from a sixteen sided drum.
Compare it with the tomb behind you, twenty years later and reaching for height instead.
This is the tomb of Isa Khan, and it has eight sides.
Walk around and count them.
The man inside worked for the king who chased the emperor Humayun out of India.
A hundred years ago this whole building was full of houses, with families living in the rooms.
In 1905 they were moved out and the garden you are standing in was made.
It is older than the big tomb behind you, by about twenty years.
The tomb of Humayun.
The survey calls it the dormitory of the house of Timur, because the emperor is not alone in here.
There are graves in the octagonal chambers on three sides of him, and the survey says five of them are of undeclared identity.
His own grave is the plainest thing in the building: a block of white marble, six feet by two feet nine, with no ornament at all.
The rooms upstairs were once a college of some importance.
Nobody recorded what was taught there or when it stopped.
The tomb of Humayun.
The dome is about seventy four feet across and it is marble over rubble, laid in alternating deep and shallow courses.
It stands on a red sandstone drum twenty five feet high, patterned with stars in yellow sandstone with black slate at their centres.
Inside, the ceiling of the central chamber is eighty feet above the floor.
Now look at the very top.
The finial is a stack of copper vessels threaded loosely on a wooden post, eighteen feet tall, taken down and put back in 1912.
It springs straight off the dome rather than from a lotus cresting, which is not how these are usually done.
This is the tomb of Humayun.
An emperor is buried in here, and so are a lot of other people whose names nobody wrote down.
His grave is the simplest one: a plain white block of marble with nothing carved on it.
The ceiling above it is as high as an eight storey building.
See the spike on top of the dome?
That is a pile of copper pots stacked on a wooden pole, and it is eighteen feet tall even though from here it looks small.
The rooms up on the roof used to be a school.
This is called the Barber's Tomb, and the survey says plainly that nobody knows why.
Two people are buried here, a man and a woman, inside the emperor's own garden.
Neither grave carries a name.
One of them carries the figures nine nine nine, which is read as the Hijri year, about 1590.
Somebody important enough to be buried in this enclosure, and all that survived of them is a job title that may not even be right.
The Barber's Tomb sits on a platform eight feet high and seventy six feet square, in Delhi quartzite picked out with red sandstone.
The chamber on top is only twenty four feet square inside.
There is a recessed arch on each of the four sides; three of them are filled with red sandstone jali screens and one is the door.
The dome stands on a sixteen sided drum with a chattri at each corner of the roof.
Go in and look up at the underside of the dome.
Traces of old blue floral painting are still there.
This is called the Barber's Tomb, and here is the strange part: nobody knows why.
Two people are buried inside and neither grave has a name on it.
One has three nines carved on it, which is a date in a different calendar.
Somebody long ago started calling it the barber's tomb and the name stuck.
Go inside and look straight up.
There is still some old blue paint on the dome.
You are inside now.
Count the columns in one bay.
There are four, and they carry one engrailed arch.
Seven of those bays make an aisle, and there are three aisles.
The recess in the east wall is where the throne stood, and the panels around it are Florentine pietra dura.
Stand over the channel in the floor.
Water ran along it the whole length of the hall and into the basin at the centre.
There are rooms underneath the west side of this building.
They were the cool ones.
Look up.
The ceiling is flat, and the arches around you are carrying it.
The dais where the peacock throne stood is the raised marble in the middle.
Run your eye along the bottom of a pier.
Each coloured petal is a separate cut stone sitting in a socket.
